newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia parliament to mull anti-NATO resolution.
newsitem.headline: Russia parliament to mull anti-NATO resolution.

text.p: Angry Russian deputies voted on Wednesday to consider a resolution declaring that Moscow would never join NATO, one day before a U.S.-Russian summit that will be dominated by the Western alliance's expansion plans.

In a separate move the State Duma lower house of parliament, dominated by the communist opposition, also decided to ask Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin to explain a radical government shake-up that has put reformers in key cabinet positions.
A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin would spend the day at his Gorky-9 country residence preparing for a meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton in Helsinki on Thursday and Friday.
The Duma voted 259-6 to weigh a non-binding resolution "On the inadmissibility of Russia's joining NATO" later in the day.

The resolution is a purely symbolic gesture since neither NATO nor the Kremlin have raised the possibility of Russia becoming part of the Western alliance. But it highlights once again the Duma's strongly anti-NATO stance.

Bitter opposition to NATO's plans to grant full membership to some eastern and central European countries is probably the only issue on which the Kremlin leader and his communist and nationalist opponents are united.

"Russia's (negative) approach to NATO expansion will not change regardless of any summits, bilateral meetings and negotiations," Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told reporters in Helsinki.
But NATO has made clear it will not drop its expansion plans to please Moscow and the Kremlin has been focusing on working out a legally binding deal to guarantee its security interests.

Moscow wants such a deal to include a NATO promise not to deploy its troops or nuclear arms on the territory of new members and a pledge never to admit former Soviet republics, including the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
But if the future document between Russia and NATO requires parliamentary ratification, as Yeltsin insists, he may find his own Duma a major obstacle.
Yeltsin, back at the helm after months of illness, has embarked on a radical reshuffle of the government, putting youthful liberals like Anatoly Chubais in charge of economic policy.
The Duma, which loathes Chubais for his pro-market views and role in Yeltsin's re-election campaign last year, has invited Chernomyrdin to the chamber on Friday to explain the changes.
But the U.S. State Department on Tuesday hailed the reshuffle as "a very positive sign".

"Here you have for the very first time the new senior economic leadership of the Russian Federation, all of whom are committed reformers, and of course, led by the greatest reformer of all -- Yeltsin," spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
Yeltsin's changes also included scrapping several ministries, including the Industry Ministry and the Defence Industry Ministry, to make government more efficient.
"Under the disguise of reorganising the government they are destroying industry, agriculture and other sectors," Interfax news agency quoted nationalist deputy Sergei Baburin as saying.
Despite its criticism of the changes, the Duma has no say in the reshuffle because it keeps the prime minister in place.
Some deputies have urged a no-confidence vote in the cabinet. If passed twice, this would give Yeltsin a choice of dismissing either the government or parliament.
But other deputies take a less hostile stance and want to wait for the new cabinet to clarify its policies.
Chernomyrdin told Itar-Tass news agency on Wednesday that the reorganisation of the government would be completed early next week.
